figures.title: Disruption rank and citations by team size
figures.caption: Larger teams generally rank lower on disruption and receive more citations, but neither pattern holds at every step. The panels show 7,933 works with a recorded reference and at least one later work citing them through 23 November 2026. On each work, at least one author listed Columbia University or an institution that OpenAlex lists under it. Panel A averages each work’s disruption percentile, its rank on a 0–100 scale among works from the same publication year. Higher ranks indicate greater disruption. The dashed line marks 50, the middle of the rank scale. Panel B shows the median number of distinct later works citing each work. Works less likely to be sampled count more. The counts below the equally spaced team sizes are the actual numbers of works. The dotted line separates individual sizes from size ranges. For the 477 works by teams of 51–100 authors, the median is 39 citing works, with a 95% confidence interval from 31 to 46 [T66]. Each bar gives a 95% confidence interval for one estimate. The intervals come from recalculating the estimates and ranks in 1,000 repeated draws within every original team-size group, including the largest. The same work could be drawn more than once in each repetition. Compare with Figure 2 of the original study [brief].

issues.problem: The caption explains how to read a disruption percentile but not what makes a work rank as more disruptive. It also leaves the set of works used for the same-year comparison implicit.
issues.fix: Add a short explanation that a work scores as more disruptive when later works tend to cite it without also citing the works it referenced. Name the set of works used to calculate the ranks within each year.

issues.problem: The caption explains how the uncertainty bars were calculated but does not say that the largest team-size group was fully sampled.
issues.fix: State that the data include every eligible work in the 51–100 author group and that its bars still show how much the estimate varied across repeated draws from those works.

figures.title: Disruption rank by team size in fields with enough data
figures.caption: Larger teams had lower estimated disruption ranks in 14 of the 20 fields and 24 of the 34 subfields that met the sample requirements. Many field intervals include zero. Only one journal met the requirements, so the result for most journals could not be tested. The field and subfield pattern was partly reproduced [T69, T70]. The dots show the estimated difference in disruption rank across works for a doubling of the number of authors. The dashed line marks no estimated difference. The score compares later works that cite the work without any of its references with those that cite both. Later works that cite only the references also count toward the total used to scale the score. The percentile is the rank of that score among works published in the same year. Works with 1–10 authors had a recorded reference and at least one later work citing them through 23 November 2026. Each had at least one author listing Columbia University or an institution that OpenAlex lists under it. Works less likely to be sampled count more in the estimates. Parentheses show actual work counts. To be included, a field, subfield or journal needed at least 30 works, at least 5 in each of the 1–2 and 5–10 author ranges, and at least 4 distinct team sizes. The second table column counts groups that met those requirements out of all groups seen in the sample. Each bar gives a 95% confidence interval for one field’s estimate. Each table range gives a 95% interval for the percentage of eligible groups with estimates below zero. The intervals come from 1,000 repeated draws within each original team-size group, including the largest, allowing repeats and recalculating ranks. The table gives each eligible group equal weight and keeps the same groups in each draw. Compare with the field comparisons in Figure 3 and Extended Data of the original study [brief].

issues.problem: The displayed title says “Disruption,” but the figure plots differences in disruption rank, not in the score itself. The axis phrase “per author doubling” is also compressed.
issues.fix: Use the same title in the image and caption, and name the rank in both. Label the axis “Difference in disruption rank when team size doubles (percentile points).”

issues.problem: The caption describes which citations count but does not explain what makes a score higher or how to read an interval that crosses zero.
issues.fix: Say that the score is higher when more later papers cite the paper without citing its references than cite both. Explain that a bar crossing zero means the data do not clearly show whether the rank is lower or higher for larger teams.

issues.problem: The phrase “including the largest” could mean the group with the most papers or the group with the largest teams. The relevant detail is that the resampling also included the group whose papers were all sampled.
issues.fix: Omit that phrase from the caption and, if needed, explain in the methods appendix that the repeated draws also included the team-size group for which every paper was sampled.

figures.title: Reference ages and citation counts in three team-size groups
figures.caption:
In the three groups shown, works with 10 or 51–100 authors cited newer and generally more highly cited references than solo works did. The two larger groups have similar citation-count curves. A lower curve in panel A means fewer references older than the age shown. A higher curve in panel B means more references above the citation count shown.

The works had at least one later work citing them through 23 November 2026. Each had at least one author listing Columbia University or an institution that OpenAlex lists under it. The curves count each reference once per work that lists it. Each link carries that work’s weight, so works less likely to be sampled count more per link, and works with more links contribute more. In order of 1, 10 and 51–100 authors, both panels use 597, 624 and 477 works. Panel A uses 22,001, 34,531 and 43,548 links; panel B uses 22,149, 34,613 and 43,772 [T75]. Reference age is the difference in publication years. Panel A includes same-year references, excludes references published in later years and shows ages through 100 years. Panel B uses current citation totals, not totals at publication. Its scale is linear through one citation and logarithmic above one.

Shading shows sampling uncertainty at each age or citation-count cutoff, not for the curve as a whole. Each 95% confidence interval comes from 1,000 repeated draws within each original team-size group. A work could be picked more than once per draw.

These curves show what we observed. They do not show whether a mathematical model fits. Separate checks ask whether a constant rate of decline describes reference age and whether very highly cited references follow the pattern the original study proposed; neither model fits closely. In the age model, a constant rate means the share of references older than a given age falls by the same fraction with each additional year. In those checks, older references became less common faster for ten-author works than for solo works. The model comparison among references with at least 50 citations was inconclusive [T76, T77]. The original finding was partly reproduced. Compare with Figure 4 of the original study [brief].

issues.problem: C5 says that the fitted reference-age and citation-count distributions both change with team size. The plotted curves show observed differences among three groups, not differences in fitted parameters. As the caption notes, neither model fit closely, and the comparison for highly cited references was inconclusive.
issues.fix: Narrow C5 to what the curves show: works with 10 or 51–100 authors cited newer and generally more highly cited references than single-author works. Report the existing model results separately: the fitted drop in the share of older references was steeper for 10-author works than for single-author works, but the comparison for highly cited references was inconclusive. Keep the plotted data and marks unchanged.

issues.problem: The phrase “logarithmic above one” names the scale but does not tell a reader how to read it.
issues.fix: Say that above one citation, each tenfold increase takes up the same space on the axis.

review.summary: The figure is clear and supports the comparison among the three groups shown. The caption appropriately calls the finding a partial reproduction. Revise C5 to match that conclusion before release; no redraw or new analysis is needed.

figures.title: Disruption rank by team size and citation rank
figures.caption:
This figure tests, but does not confirm, the original finding that the decline was stronger among highly cited papers. The decline is clear in the least-cited half; the middle and top estimates and the contrast are uncertain. Compare with the citation comparison in Figure 3 of the original study [brief].

Each point shows the average disruption percentile for one team-size and citation group. Each bar gives a separate 95% confidence interval for that average, not for the change with team size. The figure covers 7,933 works with a recorded reference and at least one later work citing them through 23 November 2026. Each work had an author listing Columbia University or an institution that OpenAlex lists under it. A work is more disruptive when later works cite it instead of citing it together with its references. Higher percentiles mean higher disruption relative to works in the sample from the same year. Citation rank compares counts of distinct later citing works among works from that same year. The middle group starts at the 50th percentile and stops just before the 90th. Works less likely to be sampled count more both when setting the groups from those ranks and when calculating the plotted averages. The legend counts each sampled work once, so the lowest half need not contain half of the sampled works. The intervals come from 1,000 repeated draws within each original team-size group. The same work could be drawn more than once, and both ranks and the citation groups were recalculated each time. The dashed line marks the middle of the disruption rank scale. The dotted line separates individual team sizes from ranges. The ranges above ten authors are shown for comparison only.

The estimates of change use teams with 1–10 authors. For each doubling of team size, the rank in the lowest citation group fell by an estimated 2.50 percentile points, with a 95% interval from a fall of 3.39 to a fall of 1.64, based on 3,277 works. In the middle group, the estimate was a fall of 1.22 points, with a 95% interval from a fall of 2.54 to a rise of 0.48, based on 2,476 works. In the top tenth, the estimate was a rise of 0.23 points, with a 95% interval from a fall of 4.33 to a rise of 3.37, based on 457 works. The estimated change was 2.73 points higher in the top tenth than in the lowest half, with a 95% interval from 1.89 points lower to 6.00 points higher, based on 3,734 works [T68].

issues.problem: The figure tests C3 but does not support it as written. Disruption rank declined clearly with team size only in the least-cited half. The most-cited tenth did not show a steeper estimated decline, and the interval for the difference is compatible with either group having the steeper decline.
issues.fix: Keep the plotted data and estimates unchanged. Present C3 as the original finding being tested, not as a reproduced result. State the result as: Among teams of one to ten authors, disruption rank fell as team size grew in the least-cited half, but the evidence did not establish a decline in the other citation groups or a steeper decline among the most-cited works.

issues.problem: The y-axis label gives the full percentile scale in parentheses, even though the plot shows only part of that scale.
issues.fix: Label the axis “Average disruption percentile” and explain in the caption that percentiles run from zero to one hundred. Keep the plotted scale unchanged.

figures.title: Distributions of disruption scores by team size
figures.caption: Most scores are close to zero. Just left of zero, the curves show that larger teams have a greater share of works with negative scores. Each curve shows the percentage of works at or below the score on the horizontal axis. The jump at zero counts only works with a score of exactly zero. The curves cover 600 solo works, 624 works by ten authors and 477 works by teams of 51–100 authors [T67]. All had a recorded reference and at least one later work citing them through 23 November 2026. On each work, at least one author listed Columbia University or an institution that OpenAlex lists under it. Works less likely to be sampled count more. A score is positive when more later works cite the work without citing any of its references than cite both the work and its references. A negative score means the reverse. Later works that cite the references but not the work also count toward the total used to scale the score [brief]. The plot shows scores from negative 0.1 to positive 0.1 and spreads out values near zero. Shading shows the uncertainty in the estimated percentage at each score separately, not for the whole curve at once. These 95% confidence intervals come from 1,000 repeated draws within each original team-size group, including the largest. A work could be picked more than once per draw. This is not a panel-for-panel redraw of the original study. Its closest comparison is the Extended Data analysis of differences in the full disruption-score distributions across team sizes [brief].

issues.problem: The caption refers to the original study’s Extended Data analysis but does not identify a specific figure or panel.
issues.fix: If [brief] identifies the closest figure or panel, give its number in the caption and keep the note that this is not a direct redraw. If there is no matching panel, say so explicitly.

C3.verdict: Partly reproduced. Among teams of one to ten authors, disruption rank declined clearly only in the least-cited half. The middle and top estimates and the difference between the top and bottom groups are uncertain. This is not confirmation of a steeper decline among highly cited works.
C3.minor_issue_type: Clarity in the image. The y-axis gives the full possible percentile scale although the visible plot shows only part of it. The axis label was outside the caption-only remit.
C3.reader_clarification: Disruption percentiles run from zero to one hundred; the plot shows only part of that scale.

C5.verdict: Partly reproduced. In the groups shown, works with ten or 51–100 authors cited newer and generally more highly cited references than solo works. These are observed comparisons only. The separate age model estimated a steeper drop for ten-author works than for solo works. Neither model fit closely, and the comparison for references with at least 50 citations was inconclusive.
C5.minor_issue_type: Caption clarity. Explain the spacing of the citation axis in everyday words. The previous note about the meaning of a constant rate was addressed and did not recur.
C5.reader_clarification: Above one citation, each tenfold increase takes up the same space on the axis.

issues.fix: Narrow the claim attached to this figure: in the groups shown, larger teams cited newer and generally more highly cited references than solo authors did. issues.problem: In the caption, “a constant rate of decline” could mean that the share drops by the same number of percentage points each year, rather than by the same fraction.
issues.fix: Say that the age model tests whether the share of references older than a given age falls by the same fraction for each additional year.

claim_scope_note: The figure gate accepts existing claim IDs only. It has no separate field for narrowing their wording. The captions state the limits of each figure, and the original C3 and C5 claim text remains unchanged. The report must mention the open issues.
method: Caption-only submissions. The submitted PDF and PNG files match the previous versions byte for byte. The three approved figures and the original files were not changed. No new analysis, external data requests, or spending.
